fetched_contents.text: Photochemical Synthesis of Gold and Silver Nanoparticles—A Review Abstract Nanomaterials have supported important technological advances due to their unique properties and their applicability in various fields, such as biomedicine, catalysis, environment, energy, and electronics. This has triggered a tremendous increase in their demand. In turn, materials scientists have sought facile methods to produce nanomaterials of desired features, i.e., morphology, composition, colloidal stability, and surface chemistry, as these determine the targeted application. The advent of photoprocesses has enabled the easy, fast, scalable, and cost- and energy-effective production of metallic nanoparticles of controlled properties without the use of harmful reagents or sophisticated equipment. Herein, we overview the synthesis of gold and silver nanoparticles via photochemical routes. We extensively discuss the effect of varying the experimental parameters, such as the pH, exposure time, and source of irradiation, the use or not of reductants and surfactants, reagents’ nature and concentration, on the outcomes of these noble nanoparticles, namely, their size, shape, and colloidal stability. The hypothetical mechanisms that govern these green processes are discussed whenever available. Finally, we mention their applications and insights for future developments. Keywords: photochemistry, nanoparticle synthesis, Au NPs, Ag NPs, green processes, mechanistic aspects, applications 1. Introduction Nanoparticles (NPs) have unique chemical and physical properties compared to their bulk counterpart due to their high surface area and outstanding electronic, optical, magnetic, and catalytic properties, to name a few [1,2,3,4]. The production of valuable nanoparticles for targeted applications is currently a fast-growing field of research [1,5,6]. Due to the ever-growing and sustained demand for nanomaterials, new and efficient synthesis methods are devised, including physical, chemical, and biological methods [6,7,8,9]. Inorganic NPs are commonly synthesized via three different approaches [10,11,12,13]. Biological methods rely on biomolecules [14,15,16,17], plants [18], fungi [19,20], yeast [21,22,23], algae [24,25,26,27,28], and living cells and organisms [29,30] to promote the synthesis of NPs [4,31,32]. On the other hand, physical methods often involve specialized equipment [33,34,35], while chemical routes usually require numerous chemicals [36,37,38,39]. To avoid using chemical compounds and generating harmful by-products, interest in developing environmentally friendly methods, such as nanoparticle photoinduced synthesis, is increasing [40,41,42,43]. In addition to being easy and simple to implement, the photoinduced method is, in many ways, a green process that relies on biological extracts [44], biomolecules [45,46], and restricted use of chemicals [47] as the reducing agent and/or the stabilizer rather than harmful substrates. Moreover, it diminishes or eliminates the generation of waste and hazardous by-products [42,48,49]. Depending on the starting material, the photoinduced synthesis can be classified as photophysical if a bulk material is downsized to nanomaterials (top–down pathway) or photochemical when atoms and molecules are assembled to build up the nanoparticles (bottom–up pathway) [42,49,50,51,52], as indicated in Figure 1. The photochemical synthesis method has comparative advantages, such as rigorous irradiation control, room temperature operation, simple and inexpensive equipment, and does not require highly skilled personnel [40,53,54,55,56]. Nanoparticle use in various fields has gained steady, growing attention, and metallic nanoparticles are no exception [57,58,59,60]. Metallic nanoparticles have a diameter between 1to a few hundred nanometers [61] and exhibit outstanding electronic, optical [62], and physicochemical [3] properties that are unique from their bulk crystal form [61,63,64]. In the past decades, silver NPs (Ag NPs) and gold NPs (Au NPs) have been extensively studied [65]. They have size- and shape-dependent properties that enable their application in numerous biological and biomedical areas [66,67,68,69], such as biosensing [70], drug delivery [71,72], medical imaging [65], and pharmaceutics [73]. Due to their antimicrobial activity [57], they are also exploited in wound dressing and healing [74]. Au NPs have superior surface plasmon resonance (SPR) properties [11], versatile surface bioconjugation [75,76], high electron conductivity [1], high colloidal stability [65], and low toxicity [72,77]. Likewise, Ag NPs possess unique SPR band [78], optical properties [79,80], good electrical conductivity, chemical stability, and catalytic properties [81] in addition to excellent antibacterial activity [82,83]. Over the years, Au NPs and Ag NPs have gained increasing importance and shown remarkable, versatile bioapplications. This review provides the readership an overview of the principal studies portraying the photochemical synthesis of Au NPs and Ag NPs using ultraviolet and visible light in addition to hypothetical mechanistic aspects, specific applications, and future developments. 2. Photochemical Processes Photochemical processes have gained significant attention in the fabrication of metallic NPs due to the enhanced spatial and temporal control these techniques offer [49,84]. A typical experiment exposes solutions containing the metal precursors to visible or ultraviolet (UV) light. Photoreduction enables controlled gold nanoparticle synthesis by using a light-driven reduction pathway that converts gold precursors into metallic nanoparticles without requiring extensive chemical reagents. The evidence indicates that photochemical synthesis is a bottom-up process in which atoms and molecules are assembled to build nanoparticles, which is different from top-down physical methods [N1-F1]. In practice, this pathway is often carried out by exposing solutions containing metal precursors to visible or ultraviolet light, which triggers the reduction of gold ions to gold atoms [N1-F1]. The review also states that photochemical routes avoid toxic or harmful compounds and do not require expensive instrumentation or highly skilled personnel, while still offering rigorous irradiation control [N1-F1]. This makes the photochemical pathway well suited to controlled synthesis.

Light intensity and wavelength are key factors that influence nucleation and growth. The evidence shows that varying LED radiation intensity and wavelength can affect the deposition of gold nanoparticles onto substrates [N3-R1]. In addition, UV irradiation at 300 nm was found to be more effective than 254 nm in inducing formation of longer gold nanorods [N3-R2]. This implies that the energy of the light, determined by wavelength, can favor different growth modes, such as elongation of nanorods, while intensity can modulate how much reduction occurs over time. The review also notes that experimental parameters such as exposure time and source of irradiation affect nanoparticle outcomes, including size, shape, and colloidal stability [N1-F1]. Together, these findings support the conclusion that light intensity and wavelength act as tuning parameters to control whether nucleation is favored, growth proceeds rapidly, or morphology becomes more anisotropic.

Photoreduction can also be spatially selective or temporally controlled because light delivery can be directed and localized. The direct laser-writing literature shows that femtosecond laser multi-photon reduction in solution can create fine particles rapidly [N6-R1]. Another example is laser-induced photoreduction of silver ions to silver atoms, which is supported by nucleation, substrate functionalization, and multiple exposure, indicating that light can be used to create features in a spatially constrained way [N6-R2]. The multi-focal laser direct-writing approach further demonstrates that spatial light modulation can enable flexible and parallel nanofabrication [N6-R3]. This spatial control is especially important because it allows the same photochemical reduction pathway to be used to generate patterned or microstructured assemblies, rather than only random aggregates. The review also emphasizes that photochemical processes offer enhanced spatial and temporal control [N1-F1], which explains why photoreduction is useful for controlled synthesis rather than bulk reduction.

Overall, the photochemical reduction pathway used in photoreduction is a light-triggered assembly of atoms from gold precursors, and the combination of intensity, wavelength, and light delivery geometry allows precise control over nucleation, growth, and spatial patterning [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

Fabrication conditions shape gold nanoparticle microstructures by imposing constraints on growth, confinement, and the spatial environment in which reduction occurs. The evidence shows that templates, substrates, and confinement can directly affect morphology. One paper reports a template-confined fabrication of controllable gold nanoparticles based on the two-dimensional nanostructure of macrocycles, demonstrating that a rigid hexagonal ring can guide nanoparticle formation and produce narrow size distributions [N4-F3]. Another study describes a template-confined fabrication pathway that enables controllable AuNPs on a surface, reinforcing the idea that templates define the available space and local chemical environment for nanoparticle growth [N4-R2]. A separate study on monolayer gold nanoparticles on SU-8 surfaces presents a simple method for selective growth of patterned monolayer AuNPs, showing that substrate chemistry and surface patterning can be used to direct morphology [N4-R3]. These examples together indicate that templates and substrates act as physical and chemical templates, controlling both size and shape.

Confinement also plays a critical role in shaping microstructures. The evidence explicitly notes that the macrocycle-based template confines gold nanoparticles into narrow size distributions [N4-F3], while the SU-8-based monolayer synthesis uses a surface platform to support patterned growth [N4-R3]. This confinement effect is not merely incidental; it alters the available space for nucleation and growth, so that particles are more likely to form in specific orientations or sizes rather than randomly aggregating. The broader review further states that the use of reagents, concentration, and irradiation conditions affects nanoparticle outcomes, suggesting that confinement is one of many process variables that can be tuned [N1-F1].

Reducing agent concentration and light exposure time are also central to controlling microstructures. The evidence indicates that the photochemical synthesis outcome depends on the nature and concentration of reagents [N1-F1]. While the direct evidence for gold nanoparticle fabrication specifically is thinner, the general photochemical synthesis review emphasizes that exposure time and source of irradiation affect size, shape, and colloidal stability [N1-F1]. For gold nanoparticle fabrication, this means that a higher reducing agent concentration can promote faster reduction and potentially smaller or more uniform particles, while longer light exposure time can favor growth over nucleation or allow more anisotropic structures to develop. In the template-confined fabrication example, the system produces narrow size distributions, which implies that both reagent chemistry and light exposure conditions are tightly coupled [N4-F3].

Spatial light delivery creates patterned or microstructured assemblies by enabling localized irradiation. The direct laser-writing literature shows that femtosecond laser multi-photon reduction can create fine particles rapidly [N6-R1]. Another example is laser-induced photoreduction of silver ions to silver atoms, which is supported by nucleation, substrate functionalization, and multiple exposure, showing that light can be used to create features at specific locations [N6-R2]. The multi-focal laser direct-writing approach further demonstrates that spatial light modulation can enable flexible and parallel nanofabrication [N6-R3]. This means that light is not only a reagent but also a tool for spatially addressing where nanoparticles form, allowing microstructured assemblies rather than uniform dispersions. In other words, the spatial delivery of light turns the photochemical process into a patterning mechanism.

Taken together, fabrication conditions shape gold nanoparticle microstructures by combining templates and substrates to constrain morphology, adjusting reducing agent concentration and light exposure time to control nucleation and growth, and using spatial light delivery to create patterned or microstructured assemblies [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3][N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

Photoreduction-based fabrication enables a range of device and functional applications because gold nanoparticles can be tuned for optical, electronic, and plasmonic properties. The evidence explicitly mentions that gold nanoparticles are used in biosensors, photovoltaics, sensors, imaging, and other applications [N5-R4]. The review also highlights that metallic nanoparticles have outstanding electronic, optical, magnetic, and catalytic properties, and that gold nanoparticles have superior surface plasmon resonance (SPR), versatile surface bioconjugation, high electron conductivity, and low toxicity [N1-F1]. These properties make photoreduction-fabricated gold nanoparticles attractive for applications such as biosensing, drug delivery, medical imaging, catalysis, and functional nanostructured materials [N1-F1][N5-R4]. The direct laser-writing literature also notes that light-assisted direct-write fabrication can generate 3D functional scaffolds with precise micro- and nanostructures [N6-R4], which expands the application space to three-dimensional architectures and scaffolds for advanced devices.

Common challenges include reproducibility, uniformity, and scaling. The review emphasizes that nanoparticle synthesis outcomes depend on experimental parameters such as pH, exposure time, and source of irradiation, as well as the nature and concentration of reagents [N1-F1]. This dependency means that small changes in conditions can produce different results, which is a challenge for reproducibility. The template-confined fabrication example shows that narrow size distributions can be achieved, but it also implies that the system must be carefully controlled [N4-F3]. In contrast, the broader evidence for photoreduction-based fabrication suggests that reproducibility may still be difficult because the method is sensitive to light intensity, wavelength, and light delivery geometry [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Scaling is another limitation: the review notes that photochemical methods are promising for facile and scalable production, but it also indicates that scaling is part of the challenge rather than a solved issue [N1-F1]. Practical fabrication methods may therefore be easier to implement on a small scale, but reproducing and scaling them uniformly across large areas remains difficult.

Compared to other nanoparticle synthesis methods, photoreduction is advantageous because it avoids toxic or harmful compounds, does not rely on expensive instrumentation or highly skilled personnel, and can be carried out at ambient conditions [N1-F1]. It also offers enhanced spatial and temporal control, which is especially valuable for controlled shape and patterned fabrication [N1-F1]. However, this method is not necessarily superior in every respect. For example, the review notes that chemical methods are widely used, and physical methods often require specialized equipment [N1-F1]. Photoreduction is more environmentally friendly and easier to implement, but it may be less versatile for all nanoparticle shapes and sizes than other methods, especially when the desired morphology is highly anisotropic or requires extreme conditions [N1-F1]. The evidence also shows that photoreduction is often used in conjunction with templates, substrates, and spatial light delivery, which suggests that it is best suited to applications where patterning and localization are important rather than where purely bulk synthesis is sufficient [N4-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2].

Overall, photoreduction-based fabrication is well suited to applications requiring optical, electronic, and plasmonic functionality, but it faces challenges in reproducibility, uniformity, and scaling [N1-F1][N5-R4]. It compares favorably to chemical and physical methods in terms of environmental friendliness and control, but its practical limits mean it is often used selectively rather than as a universal replacement [N1-F1].

## How photoreduction facilitates the controlled fabrication of gold nanoparticle microstructures

Photoreduction facilitates controlled fabrication of gold nanoparticle microstructures by combining a light-driven reduction pathway, tunable irradiation conditions, and spatially directed fabrication strategies. The result is a synthesis method that can generate nanoparticles with controlled size, shape, and pattern, while avoiding many of the limitations of conventional chemical or physical methods [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

### 1) The photochemical reduction pathway used to generate gold nanoparticles

At its core, photoreduction uses light to trigger the reduction of gold precursors into metallic nanoparticles. The evidence indicates that photochemical synthesis is a bottom-up process in which atoms and molecules are assembled to build nanoparticles, rather than a top-down physical downsizing route [N1-F1]. In practice, this means exposing solutions containing gold precursors to visible or ultraviolet light initiates the reduction of gold ions to gold atoms [N1-F1]. The review also emphasizes that photochemical routes avoid toxic or harmful compounds, do not rely on expensive instrumentation or highly skilled personnel, and can be carried out at ambient conditions [N1-F1]. This makes the photochemical pathway well suited to controlled synthesis, because the reaction is initiated by light rather than by bulk chemical reagents.

The evidence also points to direct light-directed photoreduction as a key mechanism. For example, femtosecond laser multi-photon reduction in solution is described as a method to create fine particles rapidly [N6-R1], and laser-induced photoreduction of silver ions to silver atoms is supported by nucleation, substrate functionalization, and multiple exposure [N6-R2]. These examples show that photoreduction is not just a general light-assisted reaction, but a process where light energy is used to drive the actual reduction step and can be spatially controlled [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

### 2) How light intensity and wavelength influence nucleation and growth

Light intensity and wavelength are central to controlling the microstructure of gold nanoparticles. The evidence shows that varying LED radiation intensity and wavelength can affect the deposition of gold nanoparticles onto substrates [N3-R1]. This means that intensity can modulate how much reduction occurs over time, which in turn influences nucleation and growth rates. At the same time, wavelength determines the energy available to the system and can favor different growth modes.

For example, UV irradiation at 300 nm was found to be more effective than 254 nm in inducing formation of longer gold nanorods [N3-R2]. This suggests that the energy of the light can drive anisotropic growth, elongating nanorods rather than producing more isotropic particles. The review also notes that experimental parameters such as exposure time and source of irradiation affect nanoparticle outcomes, including size, shape, and colloidal stability [N1-F1]. Together, these findings support the conclusion that intensity and wavelength are tuning parameters that can be used to control whether nucleation is favored, growth proceeds rapidly, or morphology becomes more anisotropic [N3-R1][N3-R2][N1-F1].

### 3) Why photoreduction can be spatially selective or temporally controlled

Photoreduction is especially useful because light delivery can be directed and localized. The evidence shows that femtosecond laser multi-photon reduction can create fine particles rapidly, indicating that the same photochemical pathway can be accelerated or localized by light [N6-R1]. Laser-induced photoreduction is also supported by nucleation, substrate functionalization, and multiple exposure, showing that light can be used to create features in a spatially constrained way [N6-R2]. The multi-focal laser direct-writing approach further demonstrates that spatial light modulation can enable flexible and parallel nanofabrication [N6-R3]. This means that photoreduction is not only a chemical synthesis method, but also a patterning tool.

The review explicitly states that photochemical processes offer enhanced spatial and temporal control [N1-F1]. That statement is important because it explains why photoreduction is useful for controlled fabrication rather than bulk reduction. The spatial selectivity comes from the ability to direct light to specific regions, while the temporal control comes from the ability to vary irradiation duration and intensity to control when and how much reduction occurs [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N1-F1].

### 4) How fabrication conditions shape gold nanoparticle microstructures

Fabrication conditions play a major role in shaping microstructures. Templates, substrates, and confinement are all used to constrain morphology. One paper reports a template-confined fabrication of controllable gold nanoparticles based on the two-dimensional nanostructure of macrocycles, demonstrating that a rigid hexagonal ring can guide nanoparticle formation and produce narrow size distributions [N4-F3]. ### 5) Practical applications and limitations

Photoreduction-based fabrication enables a range of device and functional applications because gold nanoparticles can be tuned for optical, electronic, and plasmonic properties. The evidence explicitly mentions that gold nanoparticles are used in biosensors, photovoltaics, sensors, imaging, and other applications [N5-R4]. The review also highlights that metallic nanoparticles have outstanding electronic, optical, magnetic, and catalytic properties, and that gold nanoparticles have superior surface plasmon resonance (SPR), versatile surface bioconjugation, high electron conductivity, and low toxicity [N1-F1]. ### 6) Integrated conclusion

Overall, photoreduction facilitates controlled fabrication of gold nanoparticle microstructures by using light as both an energy source and a spatial control mechanism. The reduction pathway is light-driven, converting gold precursors into metallic nanoparticles without requiring extensive chemical reagents [N1-F1]. Light intensity and wavelength influence nucleation and growth, with intensity modulating reduction rate and wavelength favoring anisotropic growth [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Photoreduction can also be spatially selective and temporally controlled because light can be directed and localized to create patterned or microstructured assemblies [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

Fabrication conditions further shape microstructures by imposing constraints through templates, substrates, and confinement [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Reducing agent concentration and light exposure time are also important process variables that influence nucleation and growth [N1-F1]. Spatial light delivery turns the photochemical process into a patterning mechanism, enabling microstructured assemblies rather than uniform dispersions [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].
